chapter_title: Concerning the Cross of Light: [...] trample upon it.
chapter_note: This chapter is dominated by later practical/pastoral casuistry (travel, obedience to superiors, alms-collection, elect/catechumen relations) with clear editorial fatigue in the second half. The oldest recoverable layer appears mainly as a self-contained teaching unit using the doctor/healing analogy to explain why “trampling” that causes short-term distress does not incur guilt when done for healing/liberation; one NT/Gospel saying is inserted into that teaching (overlay).

paragraphs.temporal_note: Dialogue-question apparatus (“Once again… disciple questioned the apostle”) plus explicit congregational/church setting; functions as hagiographic framing of a practical concern, not impersonal cosmological exposition.
Institutional logistics (superior, teacher of the church, foreign brethren, alms brought to church) and first-person anxiety; cosmos→church-operations application rather than cosmos→cosmos teaching.

Contains a brief frame attribution (“when the apostle heard… he says”) and then casuistic reassurance about travel ‘for the work of God’ versus ‘lustful matter’; second-person persuasion voice and ethics dominate.
Direct address and institutional identity (“Every elect and righteous person…”) with moral evaluation (crown/palm-branch vs acquisition); application voice, not structural cosmology.
Pure moral contrast (lust/body/acquisition = sin/error) without cosmological mechanism; late ethical casuistry style.
Continues practical reassurance tied to teacher-sent travel; still framed as addressing fear of sin in daily conduct.

paragraphs.core_text: because the living soul is like this. As a person, ⟨p.210⟩ if a disease will take hold of his limbs, and his heart [is sl]ow, his soul distressed, and he has pain in his disease. He seeks after a doctor to cure him, to make him strong of heart. And he cures, attends to, and gives him health [from] the disease that has risen up against him. So he thinks about this.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the opening exhortation/application address (“Again, do not be afraid even with this;”) as later pastoral persuasion leading into an older illustrative teaching.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Underlying analogy reads as general, impersonal illustrative teaching about the living soul and healing; however the paragraph opens with direct reassurance (“do not be afraid”), indicating later application grafted onto an older didactic unit.

paragraphs.core_text: [And] a wise person comes, knowing the formulas proper to a skilled doctor. If he shall achieve a healing of the one whom he [... ...] it, he recites over him the formulas that he knows, and he even tramples with his foot upon all his limbs! That person, who is ill, knows that this person is trampling upon him so that he might achieve a healing; rather, not doing this to him out of some enmity he had against him beforehand. Instead, all that he does, he does to him that he might make a healing of his body. And he expels [the] disease and the pain, trampling upon him to occasion this benefit. That person, who is ill, he can bear no anger nor hatred against this doctor, who tramples upon him. He can not hate him out of enmity, because he knows that he does this to him to his benefit.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Self-contained teaching unit: impersonal illustrative logic (healing-by-pain) with no church offices, alms, or NT citation; stays within a general correspondential analogy used to explain cosmic ‘distress’ mechanics.

paragraphs.core_text: However, should someone come and trample upon him in enmity; he may hate, prevent and not permit him! For he knows that he tramples upon him in enmity; and as he strikes out of a wanton whim, he piles another illness upon his disease.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Completes the analogy by distinguishing beneficent trampling from hostile trampling; remains within the teaching illustration without institutional pointers.

paragraphs.core_text: Again, this too is the case with the living soul; whether in the earth, or in the Cross of Light. Should you walk along upon it on the path, should you trample the Cross, it may take no reckoning against you in anger nor wrath. For it knows that [you] walk upon it for relief and healing, to proclaim on its behalf. [You] walk because of it, to reveal its mysteries. Also, the distress of the bones, which you have oppressed, befits not sin, but is set towards the victory. ⟨p.211⟩ Again, because of this nothing will be lost for you due to the distress of the bones and your toil; rather, it all accumulates to the relief (of the soul).
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the inserted NT/Gospel-style citation: “As the saviour has said: ‘Where your heart is, your treasure also will come to be there.’” (overlay entry via Gospel tradition).
paragraphs.temporal_note: Core explanatory logic about the living soul in earth/Cross of Light and ‘distress’ functioning toward victory is interrupted by an explicit ‘saviour said’ citation formula, indicating later Christian overlay inserted into an older teaching flow.
Explicit institutional scenario (teacher/foreign brethren/alms) and second-person reassurance; practical guidance about speech in church life.

paragraphs.core_text: Rather, the word that wounds is this: should a person utter a saying for the sake of the murder of a person, or the murder of animals, or for [the sake of] the murder of trees and the Cross of Light, the lying word and the wrathful and the bitter, or a word of envy and [...] only, or a word of accusation, which someone will spread against his brother; this is the [wor]d that wounds [...]. Should the person utter it, it befits [si]n; because [he has br]ought forth from it the demons [...] concerning this [...] the righteous person, or [...] all of them, which I have proclaimed, in order that [...] his word to the fetter; because anyone who would [...] his word to the fetter. And again, he [...] his coming forth, they will bind him in the place wherein he has bound his [...].
paragraphs.temporal_note: Though morally framed, it asserts a mechanistic consequence (speech ‘brings forth’ demons; binding in a ‘fetter’ and reciprocal binding-place), which reads as internal cosmic causality rather than church rule; no NT citation or institutional offices.
Returns to alms-focused application (“need of the alms… its gathering in”); institutional concern overrides any cosmological exposition.

paragraphs.core_text: [He is li]ke this, a wise doctor who might turn back [... ...] his disease. As a wound is in his body, he cuts [...] this person who is ill, in his wisdom, [...] he [...] this wound, and he cuts it. After these things [...] and he places the soluble drugs upon it, so that [they will be able to diss]olve. He might incise it with the iron, and he casts it out ⟨p.212⟩ [f]rom him, with the soluble drugs. And the wound is purified [fr]om the fever. After these events, he shall place the soothing drugs [...] and it heals up. That person, who is ill, he shall give [...] but he shall not [...] he [shall not] generate anger in his heart against him; because he knows that he is making the aspect of his benefit and his healing. After the cut that he may make, and the cauterizing that he may do there, he shall even give rewards to the doctor! He gives his thanks and is a friend to him his whole life through.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Extended, internally coherent teaching parable (cutting/cautery/drugs) explaining beneficial pain; lacks church markers and functions as a general correspondential model for ‘wounding’ that heals.

Explicitly identifies the analogy with church offices and economy (“namely the elect person… gathers it in, bringing it to the church”); cosmos→institution application dominates (editorial extension).
Institutional program for the ‘holy church’ and ascetic disciplines (prayer, self-control, chains, lashings); this is operational/pastoral material, not the older impersonal substrate.
Direct command address (“I command you, my brothers and my limbs”), catechumen instruction, and eating rules; clear late pastoral/application voice.
Dialogue attribution and summative reassurance (“Then speaks the apostle…”); functions as formal closure of the exchange.
Formulaic response of rejoicing/thanksgiving to ‘my master’; hagiographic closing typical of the Kephalaia frame.
